lead: An amplifier output has a voltage and a current; a feedback network can return a sample of either. That output choice is sampling. At the input the returned signal can subtract as a voltage in the input loop or as a current at the input node; that input choice is mixing. Two independent choices give four topologies. Mixing sets the direction of the input-resistance change; sampling sets the direction of the output-resistance change. Every topology moves both resistances, each by D. Ideal closed-loop gain is 1/β with its own unit.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for A, β and D, and Unit 2 for amplifier input and output resistance.

sections.h3: Sampling and mixing: two independent choices

blocks.text: The output carries voltage and current at once. A feedback network can return a sample of either. That is sampling.

items: Voltage sampling: the network connects across the output terminals, parallel to the load. The returned signal is proportional to v<sub>o</sub>, the output voltage. The amplifier behaves like a voltage source.

Current sampling: the network connects in series with the output loop, so load current i<sub>o</sub> flows through it. The returned signal is proportional to i<sub>o</sub>. The amplifier behaves like a current source.

blocks.text: At the input the returned signal must oppose the source. That is mixing.

items: Series mixing: the network sits in series with the input loop. The feedback voltage v<sub>f</sub> = βv<sub>o</sub> (or βi<sub>o</sub>) subtracts from source voltage v<sub>s</sub>.

Shunt mixing: the network sits across the input node, parallel to the source. The feedback current i<sub>f</sub> = βv<sub>o</sub> (or βi<sub>o</sub>) subtracts from source current i<sub>s</sub>, so less current enters the amplifier.

blocks.text: The choices are independent. Two output answers and two input answers give four topologies. Mixing sets the direction of the input-resistance change; sampling sets the direction of the output-resistance change. Every topology moves both resistances, each by D. The gain formula has the same shape, but A and β carry different units.

blocks.where: A is the open-loop gain, β the feedback factor, Aβ the loop gain (dimensionless) and D = 1 + Aβ the desensitivity.

sections.h3: The four topologies and both naming styles

blocks.text: Two naming styles are in use. The sampling–mixing name states output quantity first and input connection second: voltage-series, voltage-shunt, current-series, current-shunt. The connection name states input connection first and output second: series-shunt, shunt-shunt, series-series, shunt-series. Voltage-series and series-shunt are the same circuit.

The ideal gain comes from A → ∞: A_f → 1/β. Its unit is the topology's unit — V/V, V/A, A/V, A/A. A current-series stage gives output current for input voltage, so a transconductance amplifier uses it.

Recognisable circuits: two CE stages with a resistor from the second collector to the first emitter give voltage-series. One CE stage with a resistor from collector to base gives voltage-shunt. A CE stage with an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E gives current-series, because emitter current develops the feedback voltage across R_E.
Mixing moves R_in by D in the direction it sets; sampling moves R_out by D in the direction it sets.
R_if = R_i (1 + Aβ) for series mixing;  R_if = R_i / (1 + Aβ) for shunt mixing
blocks.where: R_i is input resistance without feedback and R_if with it. D = 1 + Aβ is the same number as in the gain formula.

blocks.text: R_of = R_o / (1 + Aβ) for voltage sampling;  R_of = R_o (1 + Aβ) for current sampling
blocks.where: R_o is output resistance without feedback and R_of with it.

blocks.text: Series mixing puts feedback voltage inside the input loop, so less input current flows for the same source voltage: input resistance looks larger. Shunt mixing pulls extra current at the input node, so input resistance looks smaller. Voltage sampling holds output voltage nearly constant against load changes: low R_out. Current sampling holds output current nearly constant: high R_out.

sections.h3: Reading a circuit in two looks

blocks.text: Identification is practical. Take two looks.

items: Look at the output. Does the feedback network connect across the output terminals (voltage sampling) or in series with the load current path (current sampling)? A resistor carrying load current samples current, even though a voltage appears across it.
Look at the input. Does feedback return in series with the source loop (series mixing) or into the input node alongside the source (shunt mixing)?
Name the topology in both styles, and write ideal gain 1/β with its unit.
Compute D = 1 + Aβ. Move both resistances, each by D, in the directions set by mixing and sampling.

blocks.text: The feedback network is not a free observer. It draws current and drops voltage, so use loaded values of A, R_i and R_o, not the bare amplifier. Rigorous analysis absorbs the network into the amplifier with two-port parameters, then applies the same formulas.

figure.caption: Sampling at the output and mixing at the input are independent choices, so four topologies exist; the two names at each leaf describe the same circuit in opposite order.

spec.aria: Tree of four feedback topologies branching from voltage or current sampling, each into series or shunt mixing.

examples.question: A voltage-series feedback amplifier has open-loop gain A = 10⁴ V/V, feedback factor β = 0.01 V/V, input resistance R_i = 10 kΩ and output resistance R_o = 1 kΩ. Find D, A_f, R_if and R_of.
steps: Voltage sampling and series mixing: R_if rises by D and R_of falls by D.
A_f = A/D = 10⁴ / 101 = 99.01 V/V, close to ideal 1/β = 100 V/V.
examples.check:
A = 1e4
beta = 0.01
Ri = 10e3
Ro = 1e3
D = 1 + A*beta
Af = A/D
Rif = Ri*D
Rof = Ro/D
print(D)
print(round(Af, 2))
print(Rif)
print(round(Rof, 2))

traps: 'Negative feedback raises input resistance' holds only for series mixing; shunt mixing lowers it. State the mixing type first.
Sampling sets R_out and mixing sets R_in. Swapping these is the most common lost mark.
Voltage-series is series-shunt. The names list sampling and mixing in opposite order, so they are one topology.
The ideal gain is 1/β but not always V/V: voltage-shunt gives V/A, current-series A/V, current-shunt A/A. A unit slip makes the answer wrong.
A resistor carrying output current samples current even though a voltage appears across it. Look at series or parallel connection, not what you measure.

quiz.q: Name the four feedback topologies in sampling–mixing style and give each ideal gain unit.
quiz.a: Voltage-series: V/V; voltage-shunt: V/A; current-series: A/V; current-shunt: A/A. Ideal gain is 1/β.

quiz.q: Which topology is series-shunt, and which is shunt-series?
quiz.a: Voltage-series is series-shunt. Current-shunt is shunt-series.

quiz.q: Why does current sampling raise R_out while voltage sampling lowers it?
quiz.a: Current sampling holds i_o constant against load changes, so output is a stiff current source: R_of = R_o(1+Aβ). Voltage sampling holds v_o constant, so output is a stiff voltage source: R_of = R_o/(1+Aβ).

quiz.q: Why is ideal gain 1/β, and why does its unit change?
quiz.a: A_f = A/(1+Aβ); letting A → ∞ gives A_f → 1/β, set by the feedback network. A and 1/β describe the same input–output pair: voltage-shunt is current in, voltage out (V/A); current-series is voltage in, current out (A/V).

quiz.q: A voltage-shunt amplifier has A = 5 × 10³ V/A, β = 0.02 A/V, R_i = 2 kΩ and R_o = 50 kΩ. Find D, A_f, R_if and R_of.
quiz.a: Aβ = 100, so D = 101. A_f = 5000/101 = 49.5 V/A. Shunt mixing: R_if = 2000/101 = 19.8 Ω. Voltage sampling: R_of = 50000/101 = 495 Ω.

quiz.q: A CE amplifier has an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E and its output is taken at the collector. Identify the topology and state how R_in and R_out change. Is it a good choice for driving a 50 Ω load?
quiz.a: The emitter current, close to output current, develops feedback voltage across R_E, and that voltage subtracts in the input loop: current-series (series-series). R_in rises by D and R_out rises by D. A high R_out holds output current, not output voltage, so across a 50 Ω load the voltage is set by the current and may run out of swing. For a low-resistance load you want a stiff voltage output, so voltage sampling (low R_out) is better.

quiz.q: A student writes: 'Negative feedback always raises input impedance and lowers output impedance.' Correct the statement topology by topology.
quiz.a: Both halves depend on topology. Input resistance rises only for series mixing (R_if = R_i D) and falls for shunt mixing (R_if = R_i/D). Output resistance falls only for voltage sampling (R_of = R_o/D) and rises for current sampling (R_of = R_o D). So every topology moves both resistances: voltage-series raises R_in and lowers R_out, voltage-shunt lowers both, current-series raises both, current-shunt lowers R_in and raises R_out. What the topology fixes is the direction, not the number of resistances that move.

beyond: Not for the exam. In IC design the same four boxes appear at transistor level: a differential pair with a current-mirror load is a transconductance stage (voltage in, current out), so feedback that senses output current and mixes a voltage in series at the input gives current-series feedback. The OTA in Unit 5 is its textbook form. Current conveyors and current-feedback op-amps use current-shunt feedback, which keeps input resistance very low and bandwidth wide. Designers replace A and β with two-port parameters of the feedback network to include loading, and RF engineers use the Cherry–Hooper technique against the unilateral-feedback limit on gain and bandwidth. In simulation, loop gain is measured with Middlebrook-style injection rather than by opening the loop. Search for 'feedback two-port analysis', 'current conveyor' and 'Cherry-Hooper amplifier'.
